items.title: 42 Gazebo Harmonic Simulation Worlds for Navigation, Exploration and SLAM workflows
items.summary: I have created 42 Gazebo & Blender simulation worlds for testing, benchmarking and improving projects that involves navigation, exploration, LiDAR and robot model setups ex. The project is open-source and licensed with Apache 2.0 so you can use it freely. Currently the worlds are 2D plan based environments with simple objects including mazes, offices, warehouses, forests, real world places, moving obstacle worlds and challenge orriented worlds. The Gazebo itself doesn’t have a good experience with creating and developing worlds so the project works via Python + Blender generation and convertion to .sdf world files. Which allows compatibility with other simulation stacks, math calculations and easier customizations to be done. I used these worlds mainly for testing my exploration project and wanted to share with you, but you can benefit from them for many various type of projects. GitHub Repository: mertgulerx/world-collection I am also planning to add 3D and textured worlds to the repository especially required for Agentic Workflows, Perception, 3D Mapping, Object Detection and Robot Training in the future but currently it is only limited to simple designs 1 post - 1 participant Re

items.title: Swift-ros2 3.0: native Swift ROS 2 client library, now with generated common_interfaces and its own org
items.summary: swift-ros2 3.0.0 is out. It is the first stable 3.x release of the native Swift client library for ROS 2 that I introduced here in April . swift-ros2 lets a Swift app join a ROS 2 graph directly, over Zenoh (round-trip compatible with rmw_zenoh_cpp ) or DDS (rmw_cyclonedds_cpp ). There is no bridge and no rcl cross-compile. What’s new in 3.0 Three packages, mirroring upstream ROS 2. items.title: robot-data-diff: episode-aware diffs for LeRobot datasets
items.summary: I built a small CLI for a problem I kept running into: you retrain a policy and it gets worse — was it the code or the data? robot-data-diff diffs any two revisions of a LeRobot dataset directly — local dirs or HF repo ids (v2.1 + v3.0). No tracking setup, no commit workflow, just point it at two dirs. It reports episodes added / removed / modified with per-episode stat deltas (frame counts, action stats, idle ratios, action spikes), plus task/schema changes and an HTML report. CPU-only, no GPU, videos never downloaded. `pip install robot-data-diff` Repo: GitHub - yafetashenafi790-lgtm/robot-data-diff: Episode-aware diff for LeRobot dataset - see what changed between two dataset revisions · GitHub Free, Apache-2.0. items.title: llm-echo 0.5
items.summary: Release: llm-echo 0.5 I'm working towards a new LLM release, and testing PRs caused me to revisit the llm-echo debug plugin. This plugin provides a "model" which doesn't involve an LLM at all - it just repeats back the prompts that have been fed to it. The new release now updates the simulated token usage counts to take tool calls, system prompts, and reasoning tokens into account. Example usage: uvx --with llm-echo llm -m echo 'hi there' -o thinking 1 --usage Outputs: First I consider the prompt, then I decide what to say. { "prompt": "hi there", "system": "", "attachments": [], "stream": true, "previous": [] } Token usage: 2 input, 24 output Tags: llm

items.title: The reverts will continue until morale improves
items.articleText: Many readers will be aware that an unusually high number of features have been reverted from the PostgreSQL 19 branch after the beta period began. Having some reverts is not unusual, maybe one per cycle could be expected. But this time around, about 8 to 10 significant features, depending on how you count, have been reverted, and some of them quite late in the beta period. I have been on the receiving end of some of that, as the developer or committer of some of those features, and have gotten some questions about it, and so I want to take a moment to reflect on this. I’ll try to extrapolate a little bit to similarly affected work that I was not actively involved in, but these are just my opinions at this point. So what happened? I don’t think we, meaning all the developers affected, have had enough time to fully reflect on all this. But here are some thoughts. It’s probably a combination of these, and a different combination in the case of each reverted feature. Maybe we just didn’t do a good enough job. Maybe the code was just not good enough. We’ll learn and improve. It’s probably some of that, and I’m mentioning it here to not give the impression that it was only the other factors that I’m going to mention. It could also be a coincidence. Maybe we had been on such a good roll that we attempted to tackle several features that turned out to be too hard, or at least too hard to finish in time. Some of the reverted features had significant architectural defects that would have been hard to fix quickly and during beta. But there was also a long tail of relatively harmless issues involving various edge cases. In past times, many of these would not have surfaced until much later and we would have fixed them bit by bit over the subsequent five years. But with LLM-assisted code review, these kinds of things can get found much faster, and then you’re staring at a list of like forty defect reports. And even if each of them requires only a three-line fix on average, there is a fixed overhead to dealing with each of these, and then you run out of time. Most if not all of the affected reverted features were written a long time ago when LLM-assisted code review was not as useful as it is now, meaning that the effective quality bar has been raised after the time the feature was written and committed. Unless the capabilities of LLM-assisted code review keep improving at the current rate, this situation should sort itself out for future development cycles. A corollary of that is that, at least for the most part, as far as I can tell, this situation is not due to “vibe coding”. This code was written well before that was a possibility. Because of the Vulnpocalypse, many senior developers were busy between, say, April (the start of feature freeze for PostgreSQL 19, and also the start of the Vulnpocalypse) and August (the most recent PostgreSQL security release) with working on fixes for security issues. Because of that, the usual additional review and testing that happens during the beta period was reduced, and then picked up again in August. That’s possibly why a lot of new issues were discovered quite late in the beta period and why so many reverts happened so late, which is what made all of this so notable. Again, some issues were more fundamental but there was also a long tail of smaller issues, and I feel with more time, say, two months, these could have been addressed (given adequate focus, but note that the Vulnpocalypse is ongoing). But the community preferred trying to stick to the release schedule rather than delaying to get more fixes in. (And you never know how long a long tail really is.) The complexity of the system has made some kinds of features extremely complex to get right, and there is not enough scaffolding in the code to support that. Consider, as an abstracted example, some SQL-level query language feature. Does it work with domains? How about with domains over a composite type? Where one of the fields is also a domain? And the domain has a not null constraint? And one of the columns was dropped and re-added? And this is part of a table partition that has been detached and reattached with a different column order? And this is part of a view that is called from a security-definer function from a trigger? And so on. No one can manually test this or even enumerate these test cases. But LLM-assisted fuzzing can find problems with this really quickly. So this probably needs to be part of feature development in the future. But we should also think about making the internal interfaces more robust so that each different combination of contexts doesn’t open up so many new possibilities of interactions. I like to say, in PostgreSQL, “everything works with everything”. This is part of the appeal, that you can construct cases like this and expect them to work. I don’t want to give up on that at all. But it does impose a significant penalty on feature development that everyone needs to be aware of. As a final point, the PostgreSQL development community has been contemplating for some time the possibility of committing features with some kind of “experimental” status and then maturing them in the main tree. This would also be one possibility to address the previous point. This would have been a helpful tool for at least some of the reverted features, but we haven’t yet figured out a way to do this, and some of the work suffered from misunderstandings related to this. This is a concrete point to work on. So what’s next? First of all, from my personal perspective, thank you to everyone who has reached out in person or online to express support and encouragement. That’s the most important thing. I’m confident that many of the reverted features will come back before too long. PostgreSQL 19 will still be a great release. REPACK CONCURRENTLY, logical replication of sequences (itself a previously reverted feature), and planner hinting with pg_plan_advice, just to pick a few headline items, will make this release very attractive. And it will be very robust, after all the additional scrutiny. It’s difficult to predict things now. A few months ago I said, PostgreSQL 20 might have no new features, just bug fixes. It turned out that things moved even faster, and PostgreSQL 19 now, kind of, has half as many major features as then expected, but now we also already have a few nice 80%-ready features queued up for PostgreSQL 20 that just need those remaining 80% to get done!

items.title: Agentic Monitoring
items.articleText: Agentic Monitoring October 19, 2026 ☸ 10 minutes A recent Anthropic blog post contained a short paragraph, not at all the point of the post, which has been buzzing around my brain since I read it: A new level of operational excellence is possible. Our team uses Claude Tag heavily, which has helped us monitor each component of the system. For example, we created Slack channels where we tasked Claude with being obsessively focused on the health of a single component. We call these Claudes “superfans.” We have a scion-daemon superfan, a scion-cache superfan, an Antique merge queue superfan, and so on. They have access to our telemetry and logs, and act like an experienced engineer who has nothing better to do than to refresh charts and look for anything strange. We also have traditional alerts for all of our systems, but our superfans can detect subtle and novel issues that make these alerts seem one-dimensional by comparison. This is so obviously the path forward for software systems operations. I’ve been thinking about monitoring with agents for the past few weeks, and this paragraph crystallized some of those thoughts. Modern software systems, like the LLMs that write them, are becoming more “grown” than “designed”. Yes, human engineers often still give the high-level design and shape to the system, and yes, software systems (for now) are much more interpretable than LLMs – since you can just sit down and read the code, if you are so inclined. However, with the volume of code being written and shipped increasing exponentially, the amount of actual eyes-on-code knowledge that any human operator of a system has is decreasing. Systems monitoring was never easy . There is a whole industry of observability SaaS companies – Sentry , Datadog , Splunk , Honeycomb , to name a few. Observability is expensive.1 Doing it well requires a specialized human skill set and relies on building experience operating real systems at scale. One can really only develop these skills by working in industry. This is a domain that takes years to train junior engineers on. As with seemingly everything in the software industry in 2026, system monitoring is poised for a step change due to agents. I… am surprised I have not seen more people write about this, especially in the current milieu of “agent frenzy”. It’s right there in front of us all, and it works . There have been a bunch of startups trying to do the “AI SRE”, but very little writing from practitioners. But you don’t really need a full “AI SRE” to improve operational excellence, nor do you need a built-out SaaS product to do so. As of the Opus 5.5 / Astra class of models, with a bit of care, it’s entirely possible to make a good agent-driven monitoring system that “just works”. Case study: change-point monitoring I’ll ground this discussion in a problem that is near to my heart: production monitoring of change points, like binary releases and config pushes . The idea is that you want to do specialized, intensive monitoring around critical points of change to a system; these change points are more likely to trigger a regression, and thus if you monitor these events closely, you can limit its impact. To quote the clichéd line from the Google SRE book, “~70% of outages are due to changes in a live system”. This is a wicked problem . I’ve been working on it in some form since 2023, and it’s been hard to get traction on. From talking with folks across the industry, I’ve learned there are ways to do change-point monitoring “well”, but these methods largely still rely on humans to do the right thing (e.g. tagging metrics/alerts diligently, defining precise signals, etc.) and require significant organizational investment. More specifically, achieving “takeoff” for change-point monitoring as a piece of platform engineering is hard because: Your first instinct may be to target highly motivated users who already have a good ops posture. However, these teams’ rollouts are already mostly safe, and you don’t actually raise the ops waterline much. The thing you’re selling here is toil reduction , which is “nice to have” but is not itself a first-order safety improvement. Precision is easier to achieve for highly motivated teams, but this means the change-point system is “competing” on recall and latency with traditional alerts. You can alternatively target the broad population of services. In other words, you go super wide and opt in “all services”, on a chosen subset of universal health metrics. In practice, most of these general health metrics are irreducibly noisy. This noise results in poor precision and alert fatigue. Prior to LLMs, there was a clear precision/latency tradeoff as well. Along this spectrum are: structured logs (precise, slow), metrics (coarse, fast), and alerts (even coarser, recall is pretty bad and precision is pretty bad, but “at least it’s something”). Shockingly, agents largely “just” solve this problem. Agents are happy to run copious queries, can write per-change queries on the fly, and will scan logs ad nauseam. As a result, you can get both good precision and recall for cheap. In the basic version of this setup, you just need the ability to connect your codebase (e.g. to reason about config consumption) and your observability stack (e.g. to view and monitor the live production state) to the agent. I’ve spiked a prototype of exactly this: an agent that proposes a monitoring plan based on the service code, a scaffold that executes that plan, and an agent that investigates triggered monitors, with an escalation path to humans. Even in this early prototype, I’ve been able to detect regressions in systems I have zero understanding of with precision and latency that would have been impossible a year ago. In my iteration on this, I’ve found that a pure agent loop is not the optimal shape for agentic monitors. Rather, a harness that allows the agent to write a spec of how to monitor, along with a deterministic system for running those specs, produces significantly cleaner signals with dramatically lower token usage. To the extent there is “secret sauce” in this pattern, it’s in the noise-reduction heuristics, the prompts that get the agent to write good specs, and a labeled eval set large enough to validate further tweaks.2 Agents are structurally well suited to monitoring Two mindset shifts need to happen before this pattern can catch on: Agents actually can do a much better job at monitoring than humans. Monitoring agents need scaffolding, the same way the rest of the software development lifecycle had to adapt for coding agents. There hasn’t been a “Claude Code moment” for monitoring yet. Once you make these shifts, monitoring agents have several “unfair advantages” over human operators: Ability to track everything, 24/7. If tokens are cheap, then any regression in a metric you care about and any suspicious log line can be investigated – not just the events that would previously have risen above the “human attention cutline”. Agents don’t need to “follow the sun” . Ability to fan out and investigate several paths toward resolving a production problem. Agents can parallelize investigations when multiple things go wrong at once, and coordinate quickly. This is already my go-to for incident triage: I just launch a bunch of agents to investigate several potential threads or theorized incident causes. Right now, this is human-driven, but there’s really no reason it couldn’t be agent-initiated in the future. You can elastically scale up a fleet of incident responders. We’re already seeing that this is becoming critical for security incidents. Teams/fleets/swarms of agents are being used for offensive cyberattacks, and defenders are beginning to build up similar defensive capabilities (e.g. OpenAI’s Daybreak Blue , Anthropic’s Project Glasswing , Google’s Fairwind ). Ability to respond faster to a problem than can a human. Agents can read code faster than humans. Agents can also query and digest metrics and log signals significantly faster. This speed doesn’t always translate into faster incident detection time; a human with a deep understanding of a system may still be faster at finding the right signal and intuiting the root causes. But to the extent that tacit knowledge can be recorded and made available to an agent, the agent will eventually beat the human on speed. By extension, for systems where the human operator isn’t deeply experienced, the “time to understanding” is going to be shorter for an agent. “A new level of operational excellence is possible.” Be more diligent: You wouldn’t pay a full-time software engineer to look through all the Git commits for a service, pick out things to monitor, and make special short-term fast-trigger alerts just on those changes. However, for a couple cents per million tokens, it’s possible now, and will become an industry standard. Continuously improve performance: Agents can monitor performance, look at heap dumps and stack traces and CPU profiles, and propose optimizations from the patterns they find. Put the proposed improvements behind A/B tests if necessary, and monitor as you would any other change to the service. In one instance, I observed that a few sessions of Astra/Opus investigation discovered 50% heap savings and 30% latency reduction in a common hot-path library that humans had already spent nontrivial effort to optimize. Once you give a sufficiently powerful LLM a VM and benchmarks to run, the “hill-climbing” ability of current-generation LLMs is remarkable. Take action : Thus far, I’ve mostly been discussing “read-only” monitoring systems. Agents, of course, needn’t be “read-only”. With the right harness and guardrails in place, there’s definitely a future in which agents will be able to take front-line actions to remediate incidents. This could span anything from well-scoped operational tasks like resizing instances or rotating compute pools, to deterministic actions like rolling back a config change or binary, to open-ended tasks like root-causing bugs, proposing fixes, and redeploying on-the-fly. Obviously there is risk the more control you hand-over to the agent, but considering how much agent capabilities expanded over the course of the past 12 months, the amount of write-path work that can be responsibly handed over to agents is bound to increase. The promise of truly self-healing systems is exciting. Cost is no longer a limitation. Luna/Haiku-class models3 are now competent graph-starers. A moderately large tech company could likely monitor its entire fleet for on the order of $100/day. Startup-scale fleets would be a small fraction of that. Compared to human labor, or even the cost of the infra that runs observability, this is trivial. Create a virtuous cycle: If done well, agentic monitoring creates a positive feedback loop: coding agents allow you to ship more, monitoring agents allow you to support more systems, which in turn frees up human time to direct more things to ship. Humans increasingly spend time “building the factory ” or “tending the garden”. Agentic monitoring is worth investing in. It will soon be reckless not to have agents monitoring your systems. Until the rest of the industry catches up, getting started now affords an unfair advantage. A set of optimizations my team recently completed saved us several million dollars in annualized observability cost, and… that was a mere fraction of what just my team spends on observability. ↩︎ Much, much more could be written about the design of agentic monitoring harnesses. This is one of the clearest “we’re so early” feelings I’ve had in a while. General harnesses, like Anthropic’s “Claude Tag”, evidently already do a good job at agentic monitoring, per the original post. However, based on what I’ve seen, even a little monitoring-specific harness engineering picks up a lot of low-hanging fruit. ↩︎ Here I mean GPT-6-Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5. ↩︎ ✉️ Subscribe via email to new posts. items.articleText: Robotics Magazine Feature Humanoid Robots The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build Agility Robotics’ first practical robotic worker is nothing like I dreamed Jonathan W. Hurst 8h 13 min read Vertical Author and Agility Robotics co-founder Jonathan Hurst next to his new Digit 5 humanoid robot worker. Christie Hemm Klok Agility Robotics , the company I cofounded out of my robotics lab at Oregon State University in 2015, has just launched Digit 5 . It’s designed to be the first humanoid robot that can safely and economically do useful work at scale, allowing us to bring tens of thousands of humanoid workers into the real world. Engineered to lift 23-kilogram bins onto high shelves and with a battery that can run for 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge, Digit 5’s goal is to handle heavy warehouse tasks shift after shift, filling the need for labor in jobs that are too physically stressful or too dull for humans to want to do. Digit 5 is what Agility has been working toward for over a decade. But the robot is heavy and bulky, lacking the graceful natural motion of its predecessors, and it’s farther than I thought possible from the robot I dreamed of building when I started this company. To deliver a useful commercial product, Agility has taken a path that is very different from what I first imagined. From ATRIAS to Digit My dream has always been to build robots that combine locomotion and manipulation to move through the world and interact with it as people do. I seek a mastery of motion, achieved through devices designed to navigate the constraints of physics with elegance. When I started the Dynamic Robotics Laboratory at Oregon State in 2008, we began with a theory derived from decades of work in biomechanics: that a simple “spring-mass” model (a body supported by legs that act like springs) should be able to reproduce every known walking and running gait found in animals. We put theory into practice by building the bipedal robot ATRIAS —short for “Assume The Robot Is A Sphere,” a joke among physicists about reducing a complex system to its simplest possible form. ATRIAS looked like a large microwave on stilts because it was only intended to demonstrate the physics of human walking and running. This was the first glimmer of achieving my dream; even though ATRIAS wasn’t designed to look like us, it still seemed natural, and even somehow alive, when it settled into a walking gait. With the success of ATRIAS, the barriers to progress shifted from scientific to engineering and organizational, and a startup company seemed like the way to bridge the gap from a one-off research concept to an actual robotic product. I felt confident of two things: that I would be able to build robots that could go where people go, and that this capability would be incredibly useful. This combination of ambition and naivete is necessary for anyone to found a new company—how hard could it be? Good advice for starting a company is to understand a customer problem, and then find a way to solve it using your unique capabilities. My cofounders, Damion Shelton and Mikhail Jones , and I did not do this. We relied on our belief that this technology would enable new possibilities and trusted ourselves to figure out the business as we went. So we simply focused on building our first product: the bipedal robot Cassie . Cassie was the first dynamic bipedal robot that researchers could buy, able to maintain its balance through active, fluid motion rather than careful, rigid steps. It had ostrichlike legs, not because we were imitating ground-running birds, but as a result of engineering strictly for performance. It was not intended to be commercially useful, and had no torso, arms, or head. We sold Cassie robots to Harvard , Caltech , the University of Michigan, the University of California, Berkeley, and a handful of other research institutions, ultimately saturating the market for US $250,000 bipedal research robots after having sold a total of 10 of them. ATRIAS, Cassie, and Digit 4 EVT [left to right] are on display at Agility Robotics’ RoboFab in Salem, Ore. The 70,000-square-foot facility has the capacity to produce more than 10,000 Digit 5 robots per year. Agility Robotics Because Cassie’s hardware enabled research into the physics of walking and running, the legged-robot research frontier shifted to control software. Traditionally, engineers controlled legged robots with detailed mathematical models that determined how the machines should move. With Cassie, researchers pioneered the new approach of reinforcement learning for bipedal legged locomotion : A simulated robot learns through trial and error, and the resulting neural network controls the physical machine. This approach is what enables virtually all of the dynamic behaviors that you see on legged robots today, and Cassie looked alive as it recovered from stumbles while climbing stairs, ran 5 kilometers across the Oregon State campus, and broke the robot world record for a 100-meter dash. Cassie got us closer to being able to move through the world with confidence and grace, but to make it useful, we needed manipulation. After exhaustively exploring different configurations, we found that an upright torso helped the robot balance, while two arms mounted near the top of the torso allowed it to pick up large objects and to catch itself when it fell. Digit 1 , which added a torso and arms to the Cassie legs, was our first mobile manipulation robot, and another step on the path toward a product that could do useful work for commercial customers. Why Digit Began With Warehouse Bins As we explored the first applications for Digit, potential customers kept asking us: Why legs? And why a humanoid? These were tough questions for me to answer, because they exposed a core business reality: It didn’t matter to Agility Robotics if we solved a cool science problem in a beautiful way. What mattered to the business was solving real problems for customers. After years of engagement with industry partners, we found one answer in warehouses and manufacturing facilities: moving bins . Bin handling is a clearly defined task where two arms are needed to lift large bins up high and legs are the best way to balance and move in narrow spaces. Because the task can vary widely from one deployment to another, it hasn’t been broadly addressed by single-purpose automation . Yet it was constrained enough to give Digit an economically viable first job while it developed a broader set of skills. In 2019, Digit began demonstrating its capabilities to do real work. With Ford Motor Company , we showed how Digit 1 could carry packages from an autonomous vehicle to a front porch. We developed Digit 2 and 3 while working with a certain global package delivery company on moving and sorting cardboard boxes. Amazon tested Digit 4 on moving and stacking bins, and it became the world’s first commercially deployed humanoid at the logistics provider GXO . In 2024, Digit appeared on the cover of Time magazine. Despite Digit’s apparent success, we began to run into conflicts between my dream and the needs of actual customers. We were no longer working with relatively patient university research labs. Agility has to sell robots to survive, and customers will only purchase robots that provide value. If bins weren’t moving, our customers were losing money. We spent a huge amount of time and effort keeping our first deployments operational, which arguably eliminated any profit we made. Yet this also kept our company learning and alive the way no lab demo ever could. I had no idea how hard it would be, or that running a company would involve so many things that have nothing to do with solving technical problems: deployments across the country; shipping, service, and customer support; fundraising and investor relations; more fundraising; human resources and IT; developing fleet-management software; managing a supply chain; and even more fundraising. I had no experience with any of these things. My career had focused on solving the technical challenges of robots interacting with the world, and it turned out that was only a tiny piece of building a successful robotics company. But Agility was the only path I saw to continuing the technical work and having an impact. Turning Digit Into a Product I knew that Agility needed to focus more on robots as a product, but I didn’t know how to make that happen. Hiring the people we needed to run the company meant giving up an immense amount of control, but we had no other choice. We recruited a new executive team with the experience required to commercialize this new technology, and they quickly made changes that were both painful and necessary. Digit versions 1, 2, and 3 [left to right] show the evolution of the robot from a dynamic walking platform into a useful mobile manipulator. Agility We had intended the next revision of Digit, Digit 4 EVT (Engineering Validation and Test), to be a relatively minor upgrade. But Agility’s new leadership insisted that the robot was missing key features that were essential if Digit was going to become a real product. So Digit 4 EVT instead incorporated a series of major changes in a highly compressed timeline, such as larger batteries and system-wide upgrades for safety and regulatory compliance, which added enough mass to dramatically alter the robot’s appearance and capabilities. While early Digits were headless, Agility Robotics was able to justify a head for Digit 4 to optimize antenna and camera placement, and it turned out to be surprisingly useful for human-robot interaction. Christie Hemm Klok I could only watch as others brought their own talents to bear to make Digit into a successful product, in gut-wrenching ways that didn’t always align with my vision. There were some especially difficult times when I felt like there were compromises made that didn’t seem necessary, but making those decisions was no longer my sole responsibility. I had to accept that Digit had grown far beyond me, and look for ways of influencing decisions rather than directing them. In the moment, it was incredibly frustrating, as Digit 4 EVT took a few steps backward from my vision of how humanoids should look and move. Agility is in our name because agility is core to the future of the company. I want Digit to be lithe and graceful. When people see Digit, I want them to like the robot, to understand what it can do at a glance, and to feel that it’s there to help. But with Digit 4 EVT, all of that was sacrificed to functionality, because of course it had to be—the customer just needs the robot to do the work. The design process became a ruthless triage, with aesthetics and elegance of movement being delayed over and over again in favor of brutal functionality. For an engineer whose mind lives more in the future than in the present, it has been hard for me to accept this trajectory. And yet, through Digit 4 EVT’s commercial deployments, we began to really understand specific applications and what they required. We mapped the first 10 use cases Digit would perform, and then began designing Digit 5 from scratch based on everything we had learned. Digit 5 Digit 5 will be Agility’s first real step toward a general-purpose robot. It marks our transition from imagining what a future humanoid robot should be to designing a product around the realities of customer deployments. These realities include things like European CE regulatory compliance, North American UL electrical-safety certifications, and Federal Communications Commission limits for electromagnetic radiation—all of which felt tangential to my dream for Digit, but were absolute requirements. Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers while working 20 hours a day and lifting more than a human can. items.title: Daimon Robotics building the infrastructure layer for tactile intelligence
items.summary: The company is connecting tactile sensing, real-world data collection, simulation, and AI models to help robots perform physical tasks more reliably. The post Daimon Robotics building the infrastructure layer for tactile intelligence appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: Credit: Daimon Robotics Vision has become central to modern robotics, but cameras alone cannot tell a robot everything it needs to know about physical contact. When handling flexible objects, inserting components, or manipulating delicate items, robots need information about forces, slippage, and contact that visual systems may miss. Daimon Robotics wants to provide the infrastructure to help robots develop that capability. Rather than focusing exclusively on tactile sensors or developing a single foundation model, the company is building a pipeline that connects tactile sensing, data collection, simulation, and AI models. Its goal is to turn physical interactions into useful training data that helps robots perform manipulation tasks more reliably. “By building tactile intelligence, we’re actually playing the role as an infrastructure provider,” Daimon’s Partner & VP of Technology Dr. Zhu told The Robot Report . “We’re not aiming to be a foundation model developer. We are providing the infrastructure for doing so for those downstream customers.” That distinction is central to Daimon’s strategy: develop the tools and data infrastructure that other companies can use to build more capable robotic systems. Building a pipeline for tactile data Collecting useful tactile data at scale presents a challenge. Unlike visual data, which can be captured relatively easily with cameras, tactile data depends on physical contact. The resulting information varies with an object’s material, geometry, the forces applied, and the task being performed. Daimon is developing a pipeline to capture and process these interactions, with tactile feedback operating at 30 Hz. The company is also working to connect real-world data with simulation, allowing physical interactions to inform training in virtual environments. The sim-to-real gap remains a significant challenge, particularly when accurately reproducing physical properties such as friction and contact forces. Daimon’s approach starts by calibrating simulations against real-world measurements before transferring collected data into simulated environments. “Let’s be frank; it’s not good enough. It’s kind of terrible,” Zhu said of the current state of simulation, referring to the gap between simulated and real-world environments. Daimon is developing tactile simulations that account for physical properties measured through real-world testing. The goal is to improve the fidelity of those simulations and make it easier to transfer learned capabilities to physical robots. The company has discussed collecting more than 10,000 hours of data, with its longer-term Daimon-Infinity initiative targeting more than 1 million hours of tactile embodied data. Zhu also emphasized the importance of working with companies developing robotic models and applications. “Doing everything ourselves was not enough,” he said. “Collaborating internationally in different downstream scenarios is really important.” That collaboration helps Daimon understand what other developers need from its sensors, data-collection devices, software, and evaluation tools. Credit: Daimon Robotics From tactile demonstrations to industrial applications Daimon is targeting manipulation tasks such as assembly and packaging, where robots must respond to physical contact rather than simply follow predetermined trajectories. A robot might need to determine whether a component is properly seated, detect when an object slips, or adjust its movements when a part behaves unexpectedly. Tactile feedback can help it respond to these conditions. The company demonstrated applications involving delicate manipulation at IROS 2026, including applying heat-transfer designs to tote bags and threading bracelets. It also showed a robot collecting and packaging broken glass, illustrating how models trained on data from varied scenarios can be prompted to perform specific tasks. Daimon uses its Umi device to collect data from human interactions. Zhu said the company’s demonstrations were powered by foundation models trained on data collected across multiple scenarios, rather than being built solely around individual robot demonstrations. The company has identified Lenovo Capital and Inovance Technology as key partners. Zhu said Daimon has also moved beyond proof-of-concept projects into industrial assembly lines and warehouses, although he declined to name specific customers because of nondisclosure agreements. The commercial test is whether tactile sensing and the models built around it can improve performance consistently in production environments, where robots must handle variations in objects, materials, and operating conditions. Moving beyond visual perception Daimon’s broader strategy centers on developing models that can use tactile information to understand and respond to physical interactions. Its Daimon-TWM effort focuses on a tactile-grounded world model intended to help robots reason about physical interactions, rather than relying on visual perception alone. Recognizing an object is only part of manipulation. A robot must also understand how its actions affect that object and adjust when the physical result differs from expectations. Tactile feedback can help close that loop by providing information about contact and the consequences of an action. Zhu described two roles for tactile sensing in robotic systems: helping models reason about physical properties and enabling rapid adjustments during contact-intensive tasks. The latter can require high-frequency feedback, with Daimon targeting control at 30 Hz. The company is also exploring how data collected through human interactions can help train models for different robot configurations, including humanoids and dual-arm manipulators. But collecting data and training models are only part of the problem. Developers must still demonstrate that these systems generalize across different objects, materials, robots, and operating conditions. Scaling touch for robotics The broader question facing the robotics industry is what infrastructure is needed to make physical AI work reliably outside controlled demonstrations. Companies are investing heavily in vision-language-action models, simulation, and large-scale robot training datasets. Touch adds another dimension, particularly for robots that must manipulate objects through physical contact. Daimon aims to build part of the infrastructure connecting sensing, data, simulation, and intelligence. Its strategy is to support the companies developing robotic systems rather than compete directly with them to build the next general-purpose robotic brain. Its success will depend on whether that approach measurably improves manipulation, reduces the effort required to develop new applications, and supports deployments across different industrial environments. Zhu was careful not to overstate the capabilities of today’s models. Even when trained on large datasets, he said, their ability to generalize remains limited. “The model is not as intelligent as we think,” Zhu said. “It has some generalization ability, but it was in-domain generalization sometimes.” He added that embodied-intelligence models are still in development, and that collecting data from similar tasks can help them generalize to new applications. For Daimon, the challenge is turning that emerging capability into reliable performance across a broader range of real-world tasks. items.title: Kodama raises $7M to bring robotics to forestry
items.summary: Kodama is working on automating forestry and logging equipment, starting with teleoperation and collecting valuable data on the way. The post Kodama raises $7M to bring robotics to forestry appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: Kodama initially focused on wildfire risk reduction in the western U.S., but it is now focusing on the timber industry in the southeastern U.S. | Source: Kodama Kodama Systems today said it has raised $7 million to bring physical AI to forestry. The company said it will use the latest funding to support commercial deployments, deepen OEM partnerships, and continue development of supervised autonomy capabilities for complex off-road environments. “Right now, we’re working with different forestry companies across the southeastern U.S,” Ben Pinfield, a go-to-market associate at Kodama, told The Robot Report . “We’re at a point where we’re scaling, integrating into new machine types, and developing more autonomy capabilities in forestry .” Kodama’s technology is already deployed in commercial logging operations across the southeastern U.S. Over the past six months, machines equipped with the company’s technology have moved more than 100,000 tons of timber across multiple states. “We’re focused on specifically plantation timber operations,” said Merritt Jenkins, co-founder and CEO of Kodama. “If we look more broadly, though, this is a tool for land management, and this is absolutely a tool that will be used in wildfire mitigation, from a forest thinning perspective, as well as wildfire suppression.” Including the latest funding, Kodama has raised a total of $14 million to date. Konvoy Ventures and Breakwater Ventures co-led the round. The round also included participation from Blue Forest Asset Management, NYA Ventures, Breakthrough Energy Ventures, Congruent Ventures, Dangerous Ventures, M1C, and others. The forestry industry faces tough conditions Forest contractors are facing a lot of challenges. Demand for timber, forest management, and wildfire-resilience work is rising, but each requires long hours at remote job sites. “If you’re a 20-something-year-old prospective logger thinking about entering the industry, you need to be on-site at 5:30 a.m., which means you’re usually leaving your home at like 4:00 or 4:30 in the morning,” Jenkins said. “Then, you’re in a machine for nine or 10 hours a day, driving over stumps and rocks and through ruts, beating up your body all day long. There are some loggers that we’ve spoken with who have gone through, for example, eight skidder operators in a year. It’s brutal turnover in this industry for this type of operator.” As fewer people go into the industry and more operators retire, it’s getting harder and harder to find experienced, reliable operators, and fewer people want to get into the industry. “For the heavy equipment operations, that [work] can be pretty rough on their bodies,” Pinfield said. “It’s like the bang just isn’t worth the buck as far as the physical trade-off for a lot of these operators. So, our customers are having a hard time hiring talent. Even when they are able to hire talent, a lot of times, it’s unreliable.” What does Kodama’s technology do on job sites? Kodama says its technology is currently running 10 to 14 hours a day on work sites. | Source: Kodama Kodama combines supervised autonomy with teleoperation , enabling machines to handle repeatable tasks while experienced operators remotely manage complex work and edge cases. The Sonora, Calif.-based company said this hybrid approach amplifies the capabilities of skilled operators and improves machine utilization. Kodama said it is currently working with skidders on logging sites. “When a group of trees are cut down, a skidder with a big claw called the grapple picks them up, and drags them to the landing where they are then loaded into trucks. It’s essentially moving these trees from one place to another,” Pinfield explained. “The ultimate goal is also working on the other machines that are in those fleets, which are the cutter and the loader.” Kodama said as it deploys more machines, its data advantage compounds through a continuous learning loop across equipment, operators, worksites, and forestry workflows. “Every day that we remotely operate the machine, we’re generating about a terabyte of training data,” Jenkins said. “Starting two and a half years ago, we took the explicit direction of starting with teleoperation, and incrementally adding autonomy, versus autonomy first with a teleoperations failover. That’s been absolutely the right decision. Now the amount of training data that we are generating across different operating environments throughout the southeast is massive.” Kodama works directly with existing OEMs Merritt Jenkins, co-founder and CEO of Kodama. | Source: Kodama Kodama is building its platform within the existing forestry-equipment ecosystem. This allows customers to adopt new operating capabilities while preserving the value of their existing machine fleets. Jenkins said the company is integrated with two of the three largest equipment manufacturers in the world. “It’s preferable to integrate with the OEMs because you can leverage all of their knowledge and all of the sensors and fault detection that are already on the machine,” Jenkins said. Autonomy retrofits are common in the construction world, but these are typically after-market kits. Jenkins said in the construction space, OEMs like Caterpillar create closed systems, so it isn’t possible to collaborate directly with the OEM. Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness! What has Kodama learned from job sites so far? Kodama has already had its technology deployed with customers in the southeast U.S. for the past two years. Pinfield said the company has been working with a customer in Georgia for over a year. “It’s always a learning process. Every logging site is a little bit different, with different terrain and a different crew that you have to work with and introduce this new technology to them,” Pinfield said. Among the biggest benefits of automation for these site operators are reliable and consistent operations. The team has also seen safety improvements with the technology. “Every person I spoke to on the logging sites has some kind of crazy story about how they know someone in the cab who flipped the machine, or got hurt, or a tree went flying. So, taking them out of the cab and having it be remote controlled or autonomous is a lot safer,” Pinfield said. Looking ahead, the company plans to expand deployments and use the data it gathers to improve productivity on job sites. “Right now, it’s several people coordinating via CB radio,” Jenkins said. “We know the real time location of our machines. We have metrics of productivity, fuel use, and the shock and vibration on the machines. So, we believe that we can eventually further optimize these sites in terms of how the machines are used and how they coordinate with each other.” About The Author Brianna Wessling Brianna Wessling is an Associate Editor, Robotics, WTWH Media. She joined WTWH Media in November 2021, after graduating from the University of Kansas with degrees in Journalism and English. She covers a wide range of robotics topics, but specializes in women in robotics, robotics in healthcare, and space robotics. She can be reached at [email protected] Tell Us What You Think! items.articleText: At a creative industry event that took place today in Berlin — hosted in collaboration with Adobe , Bertelsmann , NVIDIA and UFA — the latest advancements in intelligent media were on display. Key to the news: the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) is collaborating with NVIDIA to expand its sovereign framework with cloud, open models and integration partners, while Adobe Frame.io is accelerating video agent search capabilities with NVIDIA GPUs, helping German TV and film producer UFA find the right moments faster. Read more about both announcements below. Sovereign Clouds and Open Models Built for European Broadcasters The EBU and NVIDIA are expanding the sovereign standards they introduced last year for European public service media. The initiative now brings in sovereign cloud providers, open model developers and systems integrators to define how broadcasters can deploy agents while keeping control of their data, infrastructure, models and security. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements The EBU is the world’s leading alliance of public service media, with over 115 member organizations in more than 55 countries reaching over 1 billion people. As agents move into newsrooms, production and audience services, those broadcasters need a foundation that protects editorial independence, data sovereignty and national resilience. The expanded initiative is turning those principles into deployable services. It’ll define requirements and reference architectures for where workloads run, how data is governed, which models power services and how systems stay secure throughout their lifecycle. “These standards give EBU members a shared foundation to strengthen resilience, retain control and deliver accountable advanced services that sustain audience trust,” said Antonio Arcidiacono, chief technology and innovation officer at the EBU . Cloud providers will map the standards to sovereign deployment options: Microsoft will bring expertise from Microsoft Sovereign Cloud, including Azure Local and Foundry Local, so broadcasters can process sensitive editorial material locally and keep critical services running when external connectivity is down. Nebius offers a platform for broadcasters to train, fine-tune and run their own models on European infrastructure. Open models give broadcasters the visibility to inspect, evaluate and adapt AI for local languages, archives and editorial policies. NVIDIA Nemotron open models provide a foundation broadcasters can customize for domain-specific applications and public-service requirements. “Sovereign cloud infrastructure and open models can help Europe’s public service media innovate while protecting data, editorial independence and cultural diversity,” said Delphine Ernotte, CEO of France Télévisions and president of the EBU . Media-specific consulting and systems integration provided from Qvest and other system integrators to ensure that reference architectures are practical, interoperable and deployable in real world broadcast environments. Adobe Frame.io Speeds Video Search With NVIDIA Accelerated Computing Also at the event, Adobe is highlighting its latest enhancements that help creatives search through video data faster. Adobe is using NVIDIA accelerated computing to help creative teams find and work with video content faster. Its GPU-accelerated search pipeline uses NVIDIA NVDEC for video decoding, TensorRT for optimized AI inference and the CUDA platform for preprocessing and embedding generation. Adobe is also advancing GPU-accelerated media ingest using NVIDIA NVENC and NVDEC to accelerate video encoding and decoding, helping production teams process growing media libraries more efficiently. The results: about 5x faster embedding generation, up to 4x higher throughput and up to 5x lower latency for search processing. A new two-frame-per-second proxy, about 80% smaller than the 360p version it replaces, cuts storage and transfer while keeping the visual detail search needs. That speed matters for UFA , one of Germany’s leading film and TV producers. It delivers more than 3,500 hours of programming a year, including the daily drama “Gute Zeiten, schlechte Zeiten.” When editors build a recap or flashback, they may need a specific reaction or unresolved exchange from as far back as 15 years — something file names and folders can’t surface. Frame.io semantic search finds moments inside videos by concept, action or setting, and hybrid search adds notes, transcripts and approval status. An editor can search for “a character looking concerned,” narrow by character name and filter to approved footage, then move straight into review. The work is part of a broader Adobe and NVIDIA collaboration that also spans Adobe Substance 3D, Firefly Foundry and 3D digital twin workflows for enterprises. Learn more about NVIDIA technologies for media and entertainment . report.section_robotics:
- **Gazebo Harmonic Simulation Worlds**: 내비게이션, 탐색, 라이다 및 로봇 모델 테스트를 위해 Blender와 Python으로 생성되어 .sdf 파일 변환이 가능한 42개의 시뮬레이션 환경이 Apache 2.0 라이선스로 공개되었습니다 [1].

report.section_devtools:
- **llm-echo 0.5**: 도구 호출, 시스템 프롬프트, 추론 토큰을 반영하여 시뮬레이션된 토큰 사용량 카운트를 계산하도록 업데이트된 LLM 디버그 플러그인이 릴리스되었습니다 [6].
- **MCP Servers v2.0.0**: 레거시 클라이언트 응답 호환성을 유지하면서 최신 규격을 지원하도록 서버 패키지 전반을 리팩터링한 2.0.0 버전이 릴리스되었습니다 [9].
report.section_industry:
- **Agility Robotics Digit 5**: 23kg 적재함 리프팅과 9분 충전 후 90분 작동을 목표로 안전 규격 및 물류 현장 요건에 맞추어 설계된 차세대 휴머노이드 Digit 5가 공개되었습니다 [10].
- **Daimon Robotics 촉각 인프라 레이어**: 단일 파운데이션 모델 개발에 집중하는 대신 촉각 센싱, 데이터 수집, 시뮬레이션 및 AI 모델을 연결하는 인프라 파이프라인 구축 계획이 발표되었습니다 [12].
- **Kodama Systems 700만 달러 투자 유치**: 임업 현장에서 스키더 장비의 감독형 자율주행 및 원격 조작 상용 배포를 확대하기 위해 700만 달러 규모의 투자를 유치했습니다 [13].
- **NVIDIA 및 EBU 협력**: 유럽방송연맹(EBU)과 NVIDIA가 방송사의 데이터와 인프라 통제권을 보장하는 소버린 AI 프레임워크와 에이전트 표준 확장을 위해 협력합니다 [14].

entries.title: Daimon Robotics, 촉각 지능 인프라 레이어 구축 계획 공개
entries.reason: 접촉력과 미끄러짐을 다루는 30Hz 촉각 피드백 파이프라인 및 시뮬레이션-실제 데이터 연계를 통한 로봇 조작 인프라 개발 동향을 제공합니다.

facts.statement: Daimon Robotics는 파운데이션 모델 개발자가 아닌 인프라 제공자로서 촉각 센싱, 데이터 수집, 시뮬레이션 및 AI 모델을 연결하는 파이프라인을 구축하고 있습니다.
facts.quote: Rather than focusing exclusively on tactile sensors or developing a single foundation model, the company is building a pipeline that connects tactile sensing, data collection, simulation, and AI models.

entries.title: Kodama Systems, 임업 자동화를 위한 700만 달러 투자 유치
entries.reason: 가혹한 임업 환경에서 스키더 장비의 원격 조작과 부분 자율 주행을 결합해 물리 AI를 상용 현장에 적용하는 비즈니스 확장을 보여줍니다.

facts.statement: Kodama Systems가 임업 장비의 감독형 자율주행 및 원격 조작 상용 배포를 확대하기 위해 700만 달러의 투자를 유치했습니다.
facts.quote: Kodama Systems today said it has raised $7 million to bring physical AI to forestry.

entries.title: NVIDIA 및 EBU, 미디어 분야 소버린 AI 프레임워크 협력 확대
entries.reason: 유럽 공영 방송 연맹과 협력하여 클라우드, 오픈 모델 및 에이전트 워크플로 배포에 데이터 주권과 보안 기준을 수립하는 산업 파트너십 소식입니다.

facts.statement: 유럽방송연맹(EBU)과 NVIDIA가 방송사의 데이터와 인프라 통제권을 보장하는 소버린 프레임워크 및 에이전트 표준 확장을 위해 협력합니다.

상위 패키지(LLM 0.33)의 내부 의존성 교체에 따른 누락 종속성을 수정한 단순 패치(0.1.1)로, 새로운 기능이나 인터페이스 변경이 없습니다.

특정 소프트웨어 릴리스가 아닌 에이전트 기반 모니터링 개념 및 프로토타입에 관한 개인 블로그 의견 기고문입니다.

selectedItems.title: robot-data-diff: episode-aware diffs for LeRobot datasets
selectedItems.summary: I built a small CLI for a problem I kept running into: you retrain a policy and it gets worse — was it the code or the data? robot-data-diff diffs any two revisions of a LeRobot dataset directly — local dirs or HF repo ids (v2.1 + v3.0). No tracking setup, no commit workflow, just point it at two dirs. It reports episodes added / removed / modified with per-episode stat deltas (frame counts, action stats, idle ratios, action spikes), plus task/schema changes and an HTML report. CPU-only, no GPU, videos never downloaded. `pip install robot-data-diff` Repo: GitHub - yafetashenafi790-lgtm/robot-data-diff: Episode-aware diff for LeRobot dataset - see what changed between two dataset revisions · GitHub Free, Apache-2.0. selectedItems.summary: Release: llm-echo 0.5 I'm working towards a new LLM release, and testing PRs caused me to revisit the llm-echo debug plugin. This plugin provides a "model" which doesn't involve an LLM at all - it just repeats back the prompts that have been fed to it. The new release now updates the simulated token usage counts to take tool calls, system prompts, and reasoning tokens into account. selectedItems.articleText: Robotics Magazine Feature Humanoid Robots The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build Agility Robotics’ first practical robotic worker is nothing like I dreamed Jonathan W. Hurst 8h 13 min read Vertical Author and Agility Robotics co-founder Jonathan Hurst next to his new Digit 5 humanoid robot worker. Christie Hemm Klok Agility Robotics , the company I cofounded out of my robotics lab at Oregon State University in 2015, has just launched Digit 5 . It’s designed to be the first humanoid robot that can safely and economically do useful work at scale, allowing us to bring tens of thousands of humanoid workers into the real world. Engineered to lift 23-kilogram bins onto high shelves and with a battery that can run for 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge, Digit 5’s goal is to handle heavy warehouse tasks shift after shift, filling the need for labor in jobs that are too physically stressful or too dull for humans to want to do. Digit 5 is what Agility has been working toward for over a decade. But the robot is heavy and bulky, lacking the graceful natural motion of its predecessors, and it’s farther than I thought possible from the robot I dreamed of building when I started this company. To deliver a useful commercial product, Agility has taken a path that is very different from what I first imagined. From ATRIAS to Digit My dream has always been to build robots that combine locomotion and manipulation to move through the world and interact with it as people do. I seek a mastery of motion, achieved through devices designed to navigate the constraints of physics with elegance. When I started the Dynamic Robotics Laboratory at Oregon State in 2008, we began with a theory derived from decades of work in biomechanics: that a simple “spring-mass” model (a body supported by legs that act like springs) should be able to reproduce every known walking and running gait found in animals. We put theory into practice by building the bipedal robot ATRIAS —short for “Assume The Robot Is A Sphere,” a joke among physicists about reducing a complex system to its simplest possible form. ATRIAS looked like a large microwave on stilts because it was only intended to demonstrate the physics of human walking and running. This was the first glimmer of achieving my dream; even though ATRIAS wasn’t designed to look like us, it still seemed natural, and even somehow alive, when it settled into a walking gait. With the success of ATRIAS, the barriers to progress shifted from scientific to engineering and organizational, and a startup company seemed like the way to bridge the gap from a one-off research concept to an actual robotic product. I felt confident of two things: that I would be able to build robots that could go where people go, and that this capability would be incredibly useful. This combination of ambition and naivete is necessary for anyone to found a new company—how hard could it be? Good advice for starting a company is to understand a customer problem, and then find a way to solve it using your unique capabilities. My cofounders, Damion Shelton and Mikhail Jones , and I did not do this. We relied on our belief that this technology would enable new possibilities and trusted ourselves to figure out the business as we went. So we simply focused on building our first product: the bipedal robot Cassie . Cassie was the first dynamic bipedal robot that researchers could buy, able to maintain its balance through active, fluid motion rather than careful, rigid steps. It had ostrichlike legs, not because we were imitating ground-running birds, but as a result of engineering strictly for performance. It was not intended to be commercially useful, and had no torso, arms, or head. We sold Cassie robots to Harvard , Caltech , the University of Michigan, the University of California, Berkeley, and a handful of other research institutions, ultimately saturating the market for US $250,000 bipedal research robots after having sold a total of 10 of them. ATRIAS, Cassie, and Digit 4 EVT [left to right] are on display at Agility Robotics’ RoboFab in Salem, Ore. The 70,000-square-foot facility has the capacity to produce more than 10,000 Digit 5 robots per year. Agility Robotics Because Cassie’s hardware enabled research into the physics of walking and running, the legged-robot research frontier shifted to control software. Traditionally, engineers controlled legged robots with detailed mathematical models that determined how the machines should move. With Cassie, researchers pioneered the new approach of reinforcement learning for bipedal legged locomotion : A simulated robot learns through trial and error, and the resulting neural network controls the physical machine. This approach is what enables virtually all of the dynamic behaviors that you see on legged robots today, and Cassie looked alive as it recovered from stumbles while climbing stairs, ran 5 kilometers across the Oregon State campus, and broke the robot world record for a 100-meter dash. Cassie got us closer to being able to move through the world with confidence and grace, but to make it useful, we needed manipulation. After exhaustively exploring different configurations, we found that an upright torso helped the robot balance, while two arms mounted near the top of the torso allowed it to pick up large objects and to catch itself when it fell. Digit 1 , which added a torso and arms to the Cassie legs, was our first mobile manipulation robot, and another step on the path toward a product that could do useful work for commercial customers. Why Digit Began With Warehouse Bins As we explored the first applications for Digit, potential customers kept asking us: Why legs? And why a humanoid? These were tough questions for me to answer, because they exposed a core business reality: It didn’t matter to Agility Robotics if we solved a cool science problem in a beautiful way. What mattered to the business was solving real problems for customers. After years of engagement with industry partners, we found one answer in warehouses and manufacturing facilities: moving bins . Bin handling is a clearly defined task where two arms are needed to lift large bins up high and legs are the best way to balance and move in narrow spaces. Because the task can vary widely from one deployment to another, it hasn’t been broadly addressed by single-purpose automation . Yet it was constrained enough to give Digit an economically viable first job while it developed a broader set of skills. In 2019, Digit began demonstrating its capabilities to do real work. With Ford Motor Company , we showed how Digit 1 could carry packages from an autonomous vehicle to a front porch. We developed Digit 2 and 3 while working with a certain global package delivery company on moving and sorting cardboard boxes. Amazon tested Digit 4 on moving and stacking bins, and it became the world’s first commercially deployed humanoid at the logistics provider GXO . In 2024, Digit appeared on the cover of Time magazine. Despite Digit’s apparent success, we began to run into conflicts between my dream and the needs of actual customers. We were no longer working with relatively patient university research labs. Agility has to sell robots to survive, and customers will only purchase robots that provide value. If bins weren’t moving, our customers were losing money. We spent a huge amount of time and effort keeping our first deployments operational, which arguably eliminated any profit we made. Yet this also kept our company learning and alive the way no lab demo ever could. I had no idea how hard it would be, or that running a company would involve so many things that have nothing to do with solving technical problems: deployments across the country; shipping, service, and customer support; fundraising and investor relations; more fundraising; human resources and IT; developing fleet-management software; managing a supply chain; and even more fundraising. I had no experience with any of these things. My career had focused on solving the technical challenges of robots interacting with the world, and it turned out that was only a tiny piece of building a successful robotics company. But Agility was the only path I saw to continuing the technical work and having an impact. Turning Digit Into a Product I knew that Agility needed to focus more on robots as a product, but I didn’t know how to make that happen. Hiring the people we needed to run the company meant giving up an immense amount of control, but we had no other choice. We recruited a new executive team with the experience required to commercialize this new technology, and they quickly made changes that were both painful and necessary. Digit versions 1, 2, and 3 [left to right] show the evolution of the robot from a dynamic walking platform into a useful mobile manipulator. Agility We had intended the next revision of Digit, Digit 4 EVT (Engineering Validation and Test), to be a relatively minor upgrade. But Agility’s new leadership insisted that the robot was missing key features that were essential if Digit was going to become a real product. So Digit 4 EVT instead incorporated a series of major changes in a highly compressed timeline, such as larger batteries and system-wide upgrades for safety and regulatory compliance, which added enough mass to dramatically alter the robot’s appearance and capabilities. While early Digits were headless, Agility Robotics was able to justify a head for Digit 4 to optimize antenna and camera placement, and it turned out to be surprisingly useful for human-robot interaction. Christie Hemm Klok I could only watch as others brought their own talents to bear to make Digit into a successful product, in gut-wrenching ways that didn’t always align with my vision. There were some especially difficult times when I felt like there were compromises made that didn’t seem necessary, but making those decisions was no longer my sole responsibility. I had to accept that Digit had grown far beyond me, and look for ways of influencing decisions rather than directing them. In the moment, it was incredibly frustrating, as Digit 4 EVT took a few steps backward from my vision of how humanoids should look and move. Agility is in our name because agility is core to the future of the company. I want Digit to be lithe and graceful. When people see Digit, I want them to like the robot, to understand what it can do at a glance, and to feel that it’s there to help. But with Digit 4 EVT, all of that was sacrificed to functionality, because of course it had to be—the customer just needs the robot to do the work. The design process became a ruthless triage, with aesthetics and elegance of movement being delayed over and over again in favor of brutal functionality. For an engineer whose mind lives more in the future than in the present, it has been hard for me to accept this trajectory. And yet, through Digit 4 EVT’s commercial deployments, we began to really understand specific applications and what they required. We mapped the first 10 use cases Digit would perform, and then began designing Digit 5 from scratch based on everything we had learned. Digit 5 Digit 5 will be Agility’s first real step toward a general-purpose robot. It marks our transition from imagining what a future humanoid robot should be to designing a product around the realities of customer deployments. These realities include things like European CE regulatory compliance, North American UL electrical-safety certifications, and Federal Communications Commission limits for electromagnetic radiation—all of which felt tangential to my dream for Digit, but were absolute requirements. Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers while working 20 hours a day and lifting more than a human can. selectedItems.title: Daimon Robotics building the infrastructure layer for tactile intelligence
selectedItems.summary: The company is connecting tactile sensing, real-world data collection, simulation, and AI models to help robots perform physical tasks more reliably. The post Daimon Robotics building the infrastructure layer for tactile intelligence appeared first on The Robot Report .
selectedItems.articleText: Credit: Daimon Robotics Vision has become central to modern robotics, but cameras alone cannot tell a robot everything it needs to know about physical contact. When handling flexible objects, inserting components, or manipulating delicate items, robots need information about forces, slippage, and contact that visual systems may miss. Daimon Robotics wants to provide the infrastructure to help robots develop that capability. Rather than focusing exclusively on tactile sensors or developing a single foundation model, the company is building a pipeline that connects tactile sensing, data collection, simulation, and AI models. Its goal is to turn physical interactions into useful training data that helps robots perform manipulation tasks more reliably. “By building tactile intelligence, we’re actually playing the role as an infrastructure provider,” Daimon’s Partner & VP of Technology Dr. Zhu told The Robot Report . “We’re not aiming to be a foundation model developer. We are providing the infrastructure for doing so for those downstream customers.” That distinction is central to Daimon’s strategy: develop the tools and data infrastructure that other companies can use to build more capable robotic systems. Building a pipeline for tactile data Collecting useful tactile data at scale presents a challenge. Unlike visual data, which can be captured relatively easily with cameras, tactile data depends on physical contact. The resulting information varies with an object’s material, geometry, the forces applied, and the task being performed. Daimon is developing a pipeline to capture and process these interactions, with tactile feedback operating at 30 Hz. The company is also working to connect real-world data with simulation, allowing physical interactions to inform training in virtual environments. The sim-to-real gap remains a significant challenge, particularly when accurately reproducing physical properties such as friction and contact forces. Daimon’s approach starts by calibrating simulations against real-world measurements before transferring collected data into simulated environments. “Let’s be frank; it’s not good enough. It’s kind of terrible,” Zhu said of the current state of simulation, referring to the gap between simulated and real-world environments. Daimon is developing tactile simulations that account for physical properties measured through real-world testing. The goal is to improve the fidelity of those simulations and make it easier to transfer learned capabilities to physical robots. The company has discussed collecting more than 10,000 hours of data, with its longer-term Daimon-Infinity initiative targeting more than 1 million hours of tactile embodied data. Zhu also emphasized the importance of working with companies developing robotic models and applications. “Doing everything ourselves was not enough,” he said. “Collaborating internationally in different downstream scenarios is really important.” That collaboration helps Daimon understand what other developers need from its sensors, data-collection devices, software, and evaluation tools. Credit: Daimon Robotics From tactile demonstrations to industrial applications Daimon is targeting manipulation tasks such as assembly and packaging, where robots must respond to physical contact rather than simply follow predetermined trajectories. A robot might need to determine whether a component is properly seated, detect when an object slips, or adjust its movements when a part behaves unexpectedly. Tactile feedback can help it respond to these conditions. The company demonstrated applications involving delicate manipulation at IROS 2026, including applying heat-transfer designs to tote bags and threading bracelets. It also showed a robot collecting and packaging broken glass, illustrating how models trained on data from varied scenarios can be prompted to perform specific tasks. Daimon uses its Umi device to collect data from human interactions. Zhu said the company’s demonstrations were powered by foundation models trained on data collected across multiple scenarios, rather than being built solely around individual robot demonstrations. The company has identified Lenovo Capital and Inovance Technology as key partners. Zhu said Daimon has also moved beyond proof-of-concept projects into industrial assembly lines and warehouses, although he declined to name specific customers because of nondisclosure agreements. The commercial test is whether tactile sensing and the models built around it can improve performance consistently in production environments, where robots must handle variations in objects, materials, and operating conditions. Moving beyond visual perception Daimon’s broader strategy centers on developing models that can use tactile information to understand and respond to physical interactions. Its Daimon-TWM effort focuses on a tactile-grounded world model intended to help robots reason about physical interactions, rather than relying on visual perception alone. Recognizing an object is only part of manipulation. A robot must also understand how its actions affect that object and adjust when the physical result differs from expectations. Tactile feedback can help close that loop by providing information about contact and the consequences of an action. Zhu described two roles for tactile sensing in robotic systems: helping models reason about physical properties and enabling rapid adjustments during contact-intensive tasks. The latter can require high-frequency feedback, with Daimon targeting control at 30 Hz. The company is also exploring how data collected through human interactions can help train models for different robot configurations, including humanoids and dual-arm manipulators. But collecting data and training models are only part of the problem. Developers must still demonstrate that these systems generalize across different objects, materials, robots, and operating conditions. Scaling touch for robotics The broader question facing the robotics industry is what infrastructure is needed to make physical AI work reliably outside controlled demonstrations. Companies are investing heavily in vision-language-action models, simulation, and large-scale robot training datasets. Touch adds another dimension, particularly for robots that must manipulate objects through physical contact. Daimon aims to build part of the infrastructure connecting sensing, data, simulation, and intelligence. Its strategy is to support the companies developing robotic systems rather than compete directly with them to build the next general-purpose robotic brain. Its success will depend on whether that approach measurably improves manipulation, reduces the effort required to develop new applications, and supports deployments across different industrial environments. Zhu was careful not to overstate the capabilities of today’s models. Even when trained on large datasets, he said, their ability to generalize remains limited. “The model is not as intelligent as we think,” Zhu said. “It has some generalization ability, but it was in-domain generalization sometimes.” He added that embodied-intelligence models are still in development, and that collecting data from similar tasks can help them generalize to new applications. For Daimon, the challenge is turning that emerging capability into reliable performance across a broader range of real-world tasks.
